notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The cache multipliers that decide whether re-billed context is expensive or nearly free — Anthropic pricing: prompt caching

  • Automatic caching of a growing conversation — the mechanism behind the 79% below — Anthropic API: prompt caching

  • Published per-token prices, for the 5× output multiple — Anthropic pricing: model pricing

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • cost modeling — the cost equation and why it's quadratic in trajectory length.

  • caching in agentic systems — what prompt and tool-result caching are.

What this note adds: the arithmetic that says which factor to attack. "Cost grows with steps²" hides two factors — step count and the tokens each step adds — with different fixes and a crossover near six steps that decides which one is your problem.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two factors in the quadratic? Step count N and per-step context growth g.
Where the crossover sits? N = 2c₀/g + 1 — past it, history outweighs the prefix.
What caching the static prefix misses? The growing tail, which is the quadratic part.
Cheapest large win on a long run? Cache the whole accumulated prefix, not just the system block.
When output tokens matter most? Short runs — the 5× multiple has no N² to lose to.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I write the cost out as a sum before picking a lever, because "it grows with steps squared" hides two factors. Total input is N·c₀ + g·N(N−1)/2 — a fixed prefix billed once per step, plus the history each step re-sends. Past about six steps the second term dominates, and caching just the system prompt is then nearly pointless: you want the whole accumulated prefix cached, which takes a 20-step run from 365,000 billed input tokens to 76,000. Below six steps it inverts — the prefix and the 5×-priced output are the bill.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Cache the re-billed prefix More than ~6 steps and a byte-stable prefix. The default. Prompt-layout discipline; a TTL miss re-charges the write at 1.25×. Cache-read tokens near zero in the usage report.
Compact the context (cut g) History is bulky verbatim tool output. Information loss, plus a summarisation call of its own. Raw JSON payloads sitting in the transcript.
Cut the steps (cut N) Steps exist that code could own. Biggest lever. Scope, or engineering to move work into deterministic code. Step count varies but the work doesn't.
Squeeze output (attack the 5× line) Short runs, verbose per-step narration. Expressiveness — and reasoning quality if you squeeze thinking. Output line rivals the input line on a run under ~6 steps.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Cache the prefix Prompt assembly becomes ordered and enforced; a cache breakpoint policy appears. Input falls ~79% on a 20-step run; cuts prefill latency too. Cache hit rate becomes a live metric; slow tools cause TTL misses that show up as cost spikes.
Compact A summariser node, and a decision about what it's allowed to drop. Lowers g, so it bends the quadratic rather than scaling it. A new failure mode: the summary dropped the thing the agent needed.
Cut steps Often a workflow shape replacing part of the loop. Improves cost, latency and reliability together. Fewer spans; failures name a function rather than a step.
Squeeze output Structured tool calls instead of prose; tighter response schemas. Attacks the only 5×-priced line on the bill. Watch for quality loss that looks like laziness in eval scores.

The redraw test: caching and squeezing output change no boxes — they're rules about prompt layout and response shape. Compaction adds a box, cutting steps removes several. That asymmetry is why teams reach for the levers that redraw the diagram and skip the one that pays best.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The formula. If each step appends g tokens of model output and tool result to a fixed prefix c₀, step i bills c₀ + (i−1)g input tokens. Over N steps:

total input = N·c₀ + g · N(N−1)/2

First term linear, second quadratic. Which one you're paying is arithmetic, not opinion.

Worked instance. c₀ = 4,000 (system prompt and tool definitions), g = 1,500, N = 20:

  • Fixed: 20 × 4,000 = 80,000 · Growth: 1,500 × (20 × 19 / 2) = 285,000

  • Total input 365,000 tokens, 78% of it the growth term.

At Claude Opus 5 ($5/MTok in, $25/MTok out) that's $1.83, plus 20 × 600 output tokens = $0.30. The run costs $2.13 and the input side is six times the output side.

The crossover, which is the useful part. Growth overtakes fixed when g·N(N−1)/2 > N·c₀:

N > 2c₀/g + 1

Here 2 × 4,000 / 1,500 + 1 = 6.3. Past about six steps the history you re-send outweighs the prefix — the number that says whether "cache the system prompt" is a real answer or a rounding error. Growth is also steeper than it feels: at N = 10 the total is 107,500, so doubling to 20 steps multiplies input tokens by 3.4×, not 2×.

What caching the whole prefix is worth. With automatic caching the breakpoint advances each turn: everything already seen is a read at 0.1×, only the new block is a write at 1.25×. Each token is written once, so writes total c₀ + N·g = 34,000 and the remaining 331,000 are reads.

0.1 × 331,000  +  1.25 × 34,000  =  33,100 + 42,500  =  75,600 input-equivalent tokens

365,000 → 75,600, a 79% cut, taking the run from $2.13 to $0.68. Caching only the static block saves 0.9 × 80,000 = 72,000 of 365,000 — about 20%. Same feature, four times the payoff, decided entirely by where the breakpoint goes.

The condition on it. The 5-minute TTL refreshes on each use, so a steadily-stepping agent keeps the entry warm. A step that blocks longer — a slow tool, a human approval — lets it expire and the next step pays 1.25× again. On a run with long pauses the 1-hour TTL at a 2× write is the better trade; it pays for itself from the third read.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The first question is the one that matters, and it's arithmetic you can do on the whiteboard from two numbers the room already knows. Walking it in this order also stops the usual mistake of arriving at "use a cheaper model" before establishing whether the bill is dominated by price per token at all, rather than by how many times you re-send the same tokens.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We turned caching on last quarter and the bill didn't move."

Root cause. Two decisions, both invisible in review. The prompt assembler injected a request timestamp and session id at the top of the system block for tracing, so the prefix differed every call and nothing was ever hit — caching needs a byte-identical prefix, and nothing errors when it isn't; the request is billed at full rate and the usage fields come back zero. Underneath that, the breakpoint sat at the end of the static block, so even a perfect hit rate would only have addressed the 20% fixed term on trajectories averaging 18 steps.

Fix. Trace identifiers moved out of the prompt into request metadata, and the breakpoint moved to the end of each turn so accumulated history was cached too; cost per run fell by roughly three quarters. Applying it late cost a week of refactoring, because four features appended to the prompt in four places and the ordering guarantee had to be enforced centrally first — the expensive part was never the caching, it was that nobody owned the shape of the prompt.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You said cost is quadratic. Quadratic in what, exactly?

In the number of steps, and only through the input side. Each step re-sends everything before it, so step i bills a prefix plus (i−1) steps of history; summing gives g·N(N−1)/2. Output is strictly linear — you generate a fresh response each time and never resend it as output.

That tells you which lever bites: cutting output attacks a linear term with a 5× price, cutting steps a quadratic one. On a long trajectory the second wins by a wide margin; on a short one it barely registers.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Compaction and caching both attack re-billed context. Which first?

Caching, always, because it's lossless and compaction isn't. Caching changes the price of tokens you keep sending; compaction changes which tokens you send at all, and what you discard is something the agent may later need. Pay 0.1× for history before you pay a quality risk to delete it.

Compaction earns its place when history is bulky and low-value — a tool returning a 30,000-token payload where six fields mattered. That's a g problem, and 0.1× of an enormous number is still large. So: cache what's worth keeping, compact what was never worth sending. If you're compacting content the agent re-reads, you picked the wrong lever.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What happens to this model at 100× traffic?

The per-run arithmetic is unchanged — it's a property of one trajectory. Cache economics improve: a prefix shared across many runs amortises its write, so the effective multiplier drops toward the 0.1× read price.

The scaling trap is variance, not mean. Cost per run is O(N²), so the tail of the step-count distribution dominates the bill far more than the mean suggests. If p50 is 8 steps and p99 is 40, each p99 run costs roughly 25× a p50 run, and 1% of traffic can be a quarter of the spend. That makes a step cap a cost control as much as the reliability control §8 sets it as.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design me an agent to a target of $0.10 per run.

I'd work backwards through the formula. At Haiku 4.5 pricing ($1/MTok in, $5/MTok out), $0.10 buys roughly 50,000 input-equivalent tokens if output is a small share. With caching at 0.1× that's around 300,000 presented tokens, which at g = 1,500 supports about 20 steps — feasible on a small model with caching, and not feasible on Opus 5 without cutting the trajectory to about four steps.

That makes the decisions for me: route the loop to a small model, cache the accumulated prefix, cap steps where the quadratic would breach budget, and cost a frontier planning step separately. It also says what to measure — cost per successful run, since a cheap run that fails and is retried costs double and delivers nothing. And it's worth saying out loud that a per-run budget and a step cap are the same constraint written two ways: fix the budget and the formula hands you the cap, which beats picking a round number.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We enabled prompt caching, so context re-billing is handled."

✅ Reality: That addresses the linear term — 20% in the worked example. The quadratic term only goes away if the breakpoint advances with the conversation.

❌ Trap: "Twice the steps, twice the cost."

✅ Reality: 3.4× here. Linear intuition understates long trajectories badly, which is why a step-count estimate offered casually is usually what the interviewer probes.

❌ Trap: "Output tokens are 5× the price, so that's where the money goes."

✅ Reality: True of a single call, false of an agent. Output is linear and input quadratic, so past a handful of steps the input side is several times larger despite the cheaper unit price — six times at 20 steps here.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • cost modeling — the equation this note does arithmetic on.

  • caching in agentic systems — the caching mechanism priced here.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §10 Which cache tier, and where each one stops being safe — this note says caching is the lever; that one says which kind.

  • §10 Route by step, cascade on failure, or stay on one model — attacking price per token instead of token count.

  • §5 Restart the context or keep compacting it — compaction from the quality side rather than the money side.

  • §8 Which budgets you set — the step cap this arithmetic derives.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — long trajectories put this note's quadratic term at the centre of the cost story.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — short runs, so the answer inverts and output tokens lead.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The cascade result the whole pattern rests on — FrugalGPT: using LLMs while reducing cost and improving performance (arXiv 2305.05176)

  • What a learned router buys over hand-written rules — RouteLLM: learning to route LLMs with preference data (arXiv 2406.18665)

  • The published tier ratios that set the break-even — Anthropic pricing: model pricing

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Model routing — what cost/quality routing, cascades and semantic routing are.

  • Cost optimization — model tiering as one lever among several.

What this note adds: the break-even that decides between the two patterns — a cascade beats the frontier model exactly when the cheap tier resolves more traffic than its own price ratio, which is a number you can compute before building anything.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Cascade break-even? Resolve rate q must exceed the cheap tier's price ratio r.
What a cascade needs that routing doesn't? A cheap way to know the first answer was wrong.
Routing's hidden cost? Per-tier evals — and re-running them on every model upgrade.
What a mis-route looks like? Silent quality loss, not an error.
When neither is worth it? Uniform difficulty, or no verifier and no stable step types.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

My default is static routing by step type, because agent steps come in kinds — extraction, classification, planning — and the kind is known before the call, so I don't pay to discover it. I move to a cascade when difficulty varies within a step type and a cheap verifier exists, because then the only way to know which tier a request needs is to try. The deciding number: a cascade pays only when the cheap model resolves a larger share of traffic than its own price ratio. Below that line you've built something slower and dearer than calling the frontier model.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
One model everywhere Early, or traffic genuinely uniform in difficulty. The honest default before you have data. Frontier price on trivial steps. One model id in the code; bill flat across step types.
Static routing by step type Steps have stable, nameable kinds. The production default. A routing layer, plus per-tier evals re-run on every upgrade. A step that is always extraction running on the frontier model.
Cascade — cheap first, escalate Difficulty varies within a step type and a cheap verifier exists. Escalated requests pay both models and both latencies. Same step type, wildly different outcomes.
Learned router High volume, and rule exceptions keep accumulating. A model to train, host and re-validate whenever any tier changes. Your routing rules have more special cases than rules.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
One model Nothing — no new box. Simple, predictable, highest. One eval suite, one quality number.
Static routing A router in front of the model call; a tier table in config. Blended price = f·r + (1−f); typically 40–60% off. An eval suite per tier, and a mis-route rate to watch.
Cascade A verifier and an escalation path; the call graph gains a retry edge. Saves only if q > r; adds latency on every escalation. Escalation rate becomes the health metric — and the thing that drifts.
Learned router A trained model in the request path, with its own deploy and rollback. Best savings at scale; a fixed training and serving cost under it. Router drift on every model upgrade; it needs its own eval.

Four different call paths: one model is a straight line, routing forks before the call, a cascade loops back from the verifier, a learned router puts a second model in front of the first. That's why "we'll route to a cheaper model" is not yet a design answer.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The price ladder, which sets every ratio below. At list prices, Claude Haiku 4.5 is $1/MTok input, Sonnet 5 is $2, Opus 5 is $5 — so against Opus 5 the cheap tier ratio is r = 0.2 for Haiku and r = 0.4 for Sonnet. Output prices sit at 5× input across the whole ladder, so the ratios hold for output too.

Static routing. If a fraction f of calls go to a tier priced at r of the frontier:

blended = f·r + (1 − f)

With 70% of steps routed to Haiku (f = 0.7, r = 0.2): 0.14 + 0.3 = 0.44 — 56% off, with no latency penalty and no wasted calls. The saving is capped by f: even routing everything possible, you can't beat r itself.

Cascade, and the line that matters. The cheap model attempts everything at r; a fraction q is accepted and (1 − q) escalates and pays the frontier price as well:

cascade = r + (1 − q)·1

That beats always-frontier when r + 1 − q < 1, i.e.:

q > r

The break-even is the price ratio itself. With Haiku in front of Opus 5, the cascade pays only if Haiku resolves more than 20% of traffic. At q = 0.6 the cascade costs 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6 (40% saved); at q = 0.9, 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 (70% saved). At q = 0.15 it costs 1.05 — more than never having built it.

The term everyone forgets. If a judge call decides whether to escalate, at cost j relative to the frontier, the condition becomes q > r + j. A frontier-model judge makes j ≈ 1 and the inequality unsatisfiable — the cascade can never pay. So a cascade is a decision about whether a cheap verifier exists, not about model prices.

What the literature supports. FrugalGPT reports matching the best individual LLM at up to 98% lower cost with a cascade, or +4% accuracy at the same cost. RouteLLM reports up to 3.66× savings while retaining 95% of GPT-4's quality on MT Bench. Treat both as ceilings under favourable conditions — they depend entirely on the difficulty mix of the traffic, which is your q.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The verifier question precedes the arithmetic deliberately: without one you can't measure q, so the cascade branch isn't unattractive, it's unevaluable. Measuring q is cheap — replay sampled production traffic through the cheap tier and score it against what shipped — and belongs before any of this reaches a diagram.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We added a Haiku-first cascade to cut cost and the bill went up 8%."

Root cause. The escalation trigger was a frontier-model judge scoring every cheap response for adequacy. So the common path was cheap call plus judge call, and the escalation path was cheap call plus judge call plus frontier call — the judge alone cost about what the frontier answer would have. Nobody had written down q > r + j; the team reasoned that "most requests are easy" was sufficient justification, and it would have been, had the adequacy check been free.

Fix. The judge became a schema-and-constraint check — does the output parse, are required fields present, does the cited id exist — which costs effectively nothing and caught most genuine failures. That moved j to near zero and the cascade started paying. The late cost was a quarter of misattributed spend: routing changed alongside two other things, so it took a controlled replay to show the cascade was the regression rather than traffic growth.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Routing and cascading both send work to a cheap model. What's the actual difference?

When you decide. Routing decides before the call, from something you already know — the step type, the tool being invoked, the schema being filled — so exactly one model is called and there is no wasted work. A cascade decides after, by attempting the cheap answer and checking it, so some requests pay twice.

They suit different uncertainty. If you know a step is extraction, routing is strictly better — trying the frontier model first teaches you nothing. If the step is "answer the user's question" and difficulty varies, you can't know in advance, so paying a premium to find out is the only mechanism available.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How do you set the quality bar for the cheap tier without shipping regressions?

Per-tier evals, built before routing ships and gated in CI. Each tier gets the eval set for the step types it may serve, and a route is permitted only when the cheap tier is within an agreed delta. That delta is a product decision, not an engineering one — "Haiku may serve extraction if it's within two points of Opus on the extraction suite" is the shape of it.

This guards against the fact that mis-routing produces no error. A wrong tier returns a plausible, well-formed, slightly worse answer that nothing in the logs distinguishes. Without per-tier evals the first signal is a complaint weeks later, by which point route, prompt and model version are all suspects.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks when the provider ships a new model generation?

Every ratio moves, and so does every eval baseline. A new small model that beats last generation's mid tier inverts the ladder and changes which steps route where, so routing tables are re-derived each generation — per-tier evals are what make that bounded rather than a rewrite.

The learned router degrades worst, because its training distribution assumed the old tiers; it keeps routing confidently and wrongly with no error to alert on. That's why I'd build one only at volumes where a few percent of blended price justifies a model with its own lifecycle, and why static rules with good evals beat a stale learned router at most companies' scale.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the routing for a coding agent with a $2 budget per run.

Route by step kind first. File reads, grep, symbol lookup and diff application don't need a frontier model, and they're the bulk of steps in a coding loop; planning, diagnosing a failing test and writing a non-trivial patch stay frontier. At a 70/30 split, blended price is 0.7 × 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.44, so $2 behaves like $4.50 of frontier-only spend.

I wouldn't cascade patch-writing: the verifier there is the test suite, and running it costs more than the escalation it decides. I would cascade diagnosis if a cheap structural check exists — does the proposed root cause name a symbol that appears in the stack trace.

The part I'd put to the room is that routing interacts with caching: each tier keeps its own cache, so alternating tiers every step warms two and hits neither. That argues for routing contiguous phases rather than individual steps — a constraint you only see if cost and caching are in the same picture.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Cascades always save money — worst case you just pay the expensive model anyway."

✅ Reality: Worst case you pay both, plus the check. A cascade loses money whenever q < r + j, and a frontier-model judge makes that condition impossible to satisfy.

❌ Trap: "Route by input length — long prompts need the big model."

✅ Reality: Length proxies context size, not required capability. A one-line question can need frontier reasoning and a 30,000-token document can need extraction. Route on the step's kind or a measured difficulty signal.

❌ Trap: "We'll route to a cheaper model — that's the cost plan."

✅ Reality: Routing caps out at the price ratio, around 5× here. If the bill is dominated by re-billed context across many steps, routing rearranges a number that caching or step-cutting would have reduced by more.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Model routing — the routing mechanisms priced here.

  • Cost, Latency & Token Budget as Eval Axes — cost as an eval axis, which is how per-tier deltas get enforced.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §10 Which factor of the steps² term you attack — routing attacks price per token; that note says when token count matters more.

  • §10 Which cache tier, and where each one stops being safe — per-tier caches are why you route by phase, not by step.

  • §1 Is there a verifier — the same question decides whether a cascade is even measurable.

  • §8 What you fail over to — a cascade's escalation path and a fallback chain are the same edge drawn twice.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — classification routes down, the action step doesn't.

  • §14 Coding agent — the 70/30 phase split above is the whole cost plan.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Breakpoints, the 20-block lookback and the minimum cacheable prefix — Anthropic API: prompt caching

  • The write and read multipliers behind every break-even below — Anthropic pricing: prompt caching

  • The semantic-cache design whose similarity threshold is the whole risk — GPTCache: an open-source semantic cache for LLM applications (NLP-OSS 2023)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • caching in agentic systems — what prompt, tool-result and semantic caching are and how each works.

What this note adds: the ordering rule and the safety boundary. The three tiers key on exact bytes, exact arguments and approximate meaning respectively, and correctness risk rises in exactly that order — which is why the last one is disqualified from anything that acts.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What each tier keys on? Exact prefix bytes · exact tool arguments · approximate meaning.
When prefix caching pays? From the second use (5-min write) or the third (1-hour).
Why a cache silently does nothing? Prefix under the model's minimum, or a byte differs.
Why semantic caching can't serve actions? A near-miss returns a confirmation for work never done.
Safe TTL for a tool-result cache? Shorter than the data's staleness tolerance.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I turn them on in order of how tightly they're keyed. Prefix caching keys on exact bytes, so it can't return a wrong answer — it's the default and it goes first. Tool-result caching keys on exact arguments, so it's safe for pure reads and the only real decision is a TTL shorter than how stale the data may be. Semantic caching keys on approximate meaning, which means it can serve a response to a question nobody asked — fine for FAQ-shaped reads with a conservative threshold, and disqualified from anything that mutates state, because a near-miss there confirms an action that never happened.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Prefix / prompt caching Always, if the prefix clears the model's token minimum. Layout discipline; a TTL miss re-charges the write. Cache-read tokens near zero in the usage report.
Tool-result caching A pure read tool called repeatedly with the same arguments. Staleness — bounded by the TTL you pick. The same lookup appearing three times in one trace.
Semantic caching High-volume, repetitive, read-only questions. A false-hit rate you can tune but not eliminate. Many near-identical user questions, no side effects.
No cache Every request is genuinely unique, or the prefix is tiny. Full price on everything. Hit rates stay low however you tune them.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Prefix caching Prompt assembly becomes ordered; a breakpoint policy appears in config. Reads at 0.1×; also cuts prefill latency. Hit rate is a live metric; slow steps cause TTL misses that look like cost spikes.
Tool-result caching A cache in the tool layer, keyed on the call signature. Removes both the tokens and the downstream API call. A staleness budget per tool, and a way to invalidate on write.
Semantic caching An embedding model and vector store in the request path. Biggest saving per hit; a fixed embedding cost per miss. A threshold to tune and a false-hit rate to monitor — a new quality surface.
No cache Nothing. Highest, and honest. One less thing to be wrong about.

The first two change nothing a user could observe — they are layout rules and a lookup table. The third adds a model to the request path and a way to be confidently wrong. That asymmetry, not the saving, is what orders them.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Prefix caching pays from the second use. A 5-minute write costs 1.25× base input, a read 0.1×. For N uses of the same prefix:

uncached = N        cached = 1.25 + 0.1(N − 1)

Equal at N ≈ 1.28, so from the second use it's cheaper. At N = 10: 1.25 + 0.9 = 2.15 against 10 — 78.5% saved. With the 1-hour TTL the write is 2×, giving 2 + 0.1(N − 1), equal at N ≈ 2.1 — it pays from the third use, which is the trade for surviving pauses longer than five minutes.

The silent-failure threshold. A prefix shorter than the model's minimum is not cached at all, and no error is raised — the minimum is 1,024 tokens on Claude Sonnet 5, 512 on Claude Opus 5, and up to 4,096 on some models. The only way to know is the response: if cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are both zero, nothing was cached. Any claim about a cache hit rate that isn't read from those two fields is a guess.

Why the breakpoint position is a real constraint. You get at most four breakpoints, and the lookback window is 20 blocks — if a growing conversation pushes your breakpoint 20 or more blocks past the last write, the hit is missed. That's why long agent runs want a second breakpoint placed earlier from the start, so a write has accumulated there before the window moves past it.

Tool-result caching. The saving is hit_rate × (tool_cost + tokens_of_result) — it removes the downstream API call as well as the tokens, often the larger number if the tool is a paid API. No correctness risk provided the tool is a pure read and the TTL sits below the staleness tolerance. Inventory at 60 seconds is usually fine; account balance at 60 seconds usually isn't, and that's a product question.

Semantic caching, and the number that governs it. A hit is any query whose embedding is within a similarity threshold τ. Lowering τ raises the hit rate and the false-hit rate together; there is no setting that gives one without the other. The consequence is asymmetric: a false hit on a read returns a wrong answer, which is bad; a false hit on a write returns a success message for an action that was never performed, which is a correctness incident with a customer on the other end. Same mechanism, two entirely different severities — which is the whole reason the rule is "never for actions" rather than "tune it carefully".

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

Two questions guard the semantic branch rather than one, because "read-only" is usually asserted about the question when the risk lives in what the answer triggers. A cached response containing a confirmation, an order id or a next-step instruction is not read-only in any sense that matters, even if serving it touched no database.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A customer got a cancellation confirmation for an order that shipped."

Root cause. A semantic cache had been put in front of the agent to cut cost on a support surface where the same handful of questions dominated. The threshold was tuned on a corpus of general questions, where it performed well. But "cancel order 12345" and "cancel order 12346" are nearly identical in embedding space — the distinguishing token is a digit, which contributes almost nothing to sentence similarity — so the second request hit the first's cached response. The agent never ran, no cancellation tool was called, and the customer was told it was done.

Fix. The cache was restricted to an allowlist of intents known to be read-only, and any request whose text contained an order, account or transaction id bypassed it entirely. Applying it late was expensive in a way unrelated to engineering: the incident needed customer notifications and a manual reconciliation of every confirmation served during the window, because the logs recorded a cache hit rather than a tool call and no other record said which confirmations were real.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You said prefix caching can't return a wrong answer. Why not?

Because the key is the exact bytes of the prefix. A hit means the model is being served a prefix identical to one it processed before, so the computation being reused is computation for precisely this input. Nothing is approximated — it's memoisation of a deterministic prefix pass, not a guess about equivalence.

That's what the other tiers give up. A tool-result cache assumes the world hasn't changed since the last call, which a TTL bounds. A semantic cache assumes two different strings mean the same thing, which nothing bounds — the threshold is a business decision about how often you'll answer a question that wasn't asked.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

How do you choose the TTL for a tool-result cache?

From the data's staleness tolerance, not the hit rate — that's the direction where being wrong is cheap. Start from what the consumer tolerates, then accept whatever hit rate that TTL produces. Choosing a TTL to hit a cost target inverts the dependency and eventually serves a stale answer that matters.

Most tools have two tolerances rather than one: a catalogue tolerates minutes for browsing and zero for the price check at checkout. That means the same underlying call often needs two entry points with different caching, and noticing it in the round is worth more than any TTL number you could name.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What happens to caching at 100× traffic?

Prefix caching improves — a shared prefix's write amortises across far more reads, pushing the effective multiplier toward 0.1×. The benefit distributes unevenly though: a high-traffic tenant always finds a warm cache while a low-traffic one may never hit within the TTL, so two customers see different latency and cost for the same workload. Worth knowing before it arrives as a bug report.

Semantic caching gets more dangerous rather than cheaper. The false-hit rate is fixed by the threshold, so the false-hit count scales linearly — at 100× you get 100× the wrong answers from a component validated when a handful a day was tolerable. Any threshold justified by "we only saw two bad hits in testing" needs re-deriving as an absolute number at production volume.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design caching for a multi-tenant agent platform.

Prefix caching first, with the prompt laid out platform-static, then tenant-static, then run-specific. That ordering shares the platform prefix across every tenant while each tenant's configuration forms a second cached segment — one of the reasons for multiple breakpoints.

Tool-result caching must be keyed by tenant, always, even where the tool looks global. The failure here isn't stale data, it's a key that omits the tenant and serves one customer's lookup to another — the same class of bug as a missing WHERE tenant_id, with none of the review attention a SQL query would get.

Semantic caching defaults off, scoped per tenant if a customer asks for it. A threshold safe for one tenant's question distribution isn't safe for another's, and a shared semantic cache across tenants is a data-isolation problem wearing a cost-optimisation hat.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Caching is enabled, so we're getting the discount."

✅ Reality: Nothing errors when a cache misses. A prefix under the model's minimum, or one byte of drift, silently bills at full rate. Read cache_read_input_tokens or you don't know.

❌ Trap: "Semantic caching is just caching with better matching."

✅ Reality: It's the only tier that can return a response to a question nobody asked. That's a quality surface, not an infrastructure optimisation, and it never goes in front of anything that acts.

❌ Trap: "Put the cache breakpoint after the system prompt and you're done."

✅ Reality: On a long run that caches the small fixed term and misses the growing one. And with a 20-block lookback, a single breakpoint left behind by a growing conversation stops hitting altogether.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • caching in agentic systems — the three mechanisms this note orders and bounds.

  • Cost optimization — caching among the other cost levers.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §10 Which factor of the steps² term you attack — where breakpoint placement is worth 79% rather than 20%.

  • §10 Route by step, cascade on failure, or stay on one model — per-tier caches are why routing works better by phase than by step.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — the same read/write line decides what a tool-result cache may serve.

  • §9 Which term in the latency sum you attack — prefix caching is the one lever that cuts cost and time together.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the semantic-cache boundary is the centre of the cost story.

  • §14 Deep research agent — long runs make breakpoint placement the dominant decision.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The scope ladder a gateway actually offers, and what it returns on a trip — LiteLLM proxy: budgets and rate limits

  • The reporting lag that disqualifies billing APIs as an enforcement point — Anthropic: Usage and Cost Admin API

  • The per-response usage fields a gateway meters from — Anthropic pricing: prompt caching

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Rate limiting quota & API-level multi-tenancy — quota, rate limiting and per-tenant isolation at the API layer.

  • cost modeling — what a run costs, which is what the cap is denominated in.

What this note adds: the enforcement-point argument. A cap binds only where spend is counted, which rules out the prompt entirely and rules out the provider's billing API for anything real-time — and the per-run cap everyone reaches for doesn't bound a tenant at all.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why never in the prompt? The model has no billing state — it can't count its own spend.
Minimum viable set of scopes? Per run and per tenant. One alone bounds nothing useful.
Worst-case tenant exposure? Per-run cap × max concurrent runs.
Why not read the provider's billing API? It lags minutes; the cost endpoint is daily.
What a trip needs besides a 429? A graceful branch — same one the step cap needs.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Caps go in the gateway, because a cap binds only where the spend is counted, and the gateway is the one place that sees every call from every run. The prompt is disqualified outright — the model has no access to its own billing state, so "stay under five dollars" is a wish. And I always set at least two scopes, because a per-run cap bounds one runaway and nothing else: multiply it by how many runs a tenant can start concurrently and that's your real exposure. The pivot is that the tighter the cap, the more it needs a graceful branch, or you've converted a cost problem into an outage.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
In the prompt Never. It is not an enforcement point. Nothing — and it enforces nothing. A system prompt containing a dollar figure.
In the harness (per run) Always, as the inner bound on one trajectory. Only binds in-process; a crashed harness stops counting. A step cap exists but no token or spend equivalent.
In the gateway Anything multi-tenant or multi-feature. The default. A proxy in the hot path, and its own availability story. Spend attributable per call but not bounded per customer.
At the provider account As the last-resort ceiling on the whole org. Blunt — it stops everyone, including production, at once. You want a bound that survives your own bugs.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Harness cap A running token tally in the loop; a trip branch beside the step cap. Bounds one run. Says nothing about aggregate. Per-run cost gets a hard ceiling you can quote.
Gateway cap A proxy every call routes through; virtual keys per tenant or feature. Bounds tenant and feature spend; enables chargeback. The proxy becomes a dependency with its own SLO and failure mode.
Provider cap None in your system. An org-wide ceiling. When it trips, everything stops — including whatever was healthy.
Prompt "cap" None. None. A false sense of control, which is worse than none.

The gateway is the only row that adds a box, and it's the box that makes per-tenant cost a number you can produce on demand rather than reconstruct from an invoice. That's usually what sells it internally: the cap is the safety property, attribution is the daily benefit.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why a per-run cap doesn't bound a tenant. With a per-run cap C and a maximum of K concurrent runs per tenant:

worst-case tenant exposure = C × K

At C = $2 and K = 500 concurrent runs, that's $1,000 of exposure from a cap that looks tight. And K is rarely a designed number — it's whatever the queue and the retry policy permit, which is usually unbounded until someone measures it. A per-run cap without a concurrency bound or a tenant cap is a ceiling on the wrong axis.

Why the enforcement point must count locally. A gateway meters from the usage block of each response — input, output, cache-read and cache-creation tokens — and prices them itself. The alternative, reading the provider's billing API, doesn't work for enforcement: usage data typically appears within about five minutes of a request completing, and the cost endpoint has daily granularity only. Five minutes of unbounded agent traffic is the entire incident. Billing APIs are for reconciliation, not for control.

What the scope ladder looks like in practice. A production gateway exposes budgets at global proxy, team, team member, internal user, virtual key, end-customer and agent-session level, and rejects an over-budget call with an authentication or rate-limit error. The design question is not what's available but which two or three you actually set — and the pairing that covers the common failures is per-run (bounds a loop), per-tenant-per-day (bounds a customer), and per-feature (bounds a bad deploy).

The cost of the check itself. The gateway adds a synchronous hop on every model call. If it adds d milliseconds and a run makes N calls, the run pays N·d — at N = 20 and d = 5ms, 100ms per run, which is noise against a multi-second trajectory. Worth stating explicitly, because the objection is common and the arithmetic dismisses it.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The terminal question is the one people skip. A cap is a decision about what happens at the boundary, not just where the boundary sits — and a gateway that returns a 429 mid-trajectory hands the agent an error it will probably retry into, which is how a spend cap becomes a spend amplifier.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The monthly bill was four times forecast, and the budget alert fired on the 3rd."

Root cause. Budgets were a scheduled job that polled the provider's cost endpoint and disabled keys when a tenant passed its allocation. Two properties killed it: the cost endpoint reports daily, so the job could only act on yesterday's spend, and a retry loop in one tenant's integration restarted failed runs continuously overnight, each individually well under the per-run cap. By the time the job saw the number the money was spent — the control was a report with a cron schedule attached.

Fix. Metering moved into the gateway, counting tokens from each response's usage block and pricing them in-process, with per-tenant daily budgets enforced synchronously on the request path. The provider's cost API stayed, in the role it's suited to: end-of-day reconciliation against what the gateway thought it had spent. The late-application cost was that every caller had to be moved behind the proxy, and three internal services were calling the provider directly with the org key — which is the same reason the cap hadn't existed in the first place.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

What's actually wrong with putting a budget in the system prompt?

The model has no access to its own billing state. It cannot observe how many tokens it has consumed this run, what they cost, or what the run has spent so far — none of that is in its context unless you put it there, and even then it's a number in text that the model may or may not respect. There's no mechanism by which an instruction becomes a constraint.

It also fails the basic test for a control: nothing should be able to argue past it. Anything in the prompt is subject to the same instruction-following as everything else there, so it's a preference at best. Controls live where spend is counted — your harness, your gateway, the provider.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Harness or gateway — why not just the harness, which is simpler?

The harness is simpler and it's the right place for the per-run bound, because it holds the run's state and can stop cleanly mid-trajectory with a partial answer. What it can't do is see any other run. Every aggregate question — what has this tenant spent today, is this feature's spend anomalous, has this API key run away — is invisible from inside one process.

There's also a survivability difference: a harness that crashes stops counting, and whatever was in flight goes unaccounted for, whereas a gateway counts on the request path so nothing gets past it by dying. I'd run both, harness cap below gateway cap, so the common case trips where it can degrade gracefully and the gateway backstops everything the harness didn't survive to enforce.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks when the cap trips at 100× traffic?

The retry interaction. A budget rejection arrives as a 429 or 401, which generic clients treat as retryable, so a tripped cap can generate more requests than it prevents — each cheap to reject but not free. Budget rejections must be distinguishable from throttling and treated as terminal.

The second is that budgets are shared state, so synchronous enforcement means a read-modify-write on a hot counter per request. At high concurrency an exactly-correct counter becomes the bottleneck, and the usual resolution is a small accepted overshoot from periodically-flushed local counters. A budget enforced to within a percent is a real control; the mistake is believing it's exact when it's eventually consistent.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design spend control for a platform where customers bring their own agents.

Three layers. A per-run cap in the harness, set from the customer's plan, that degrades to a partial answer. A per-customer daily budget in the gateway on a virtual key, enforced synchronously and rejecting terminally rather than retryably. An org-level ceiling at the provider as the backstop against my own bugs, because the gateway is code I wrote and the cap that matters most shouldn't depend on it being correct.

Concurrency is the fourth control and the easiest to miss: without a bound on concurrent runs per customer, the per-run cap multiplies by an unbounded number, so a concurrency lease sits alongside the budget and the two together make exposure calculable.

The part I'd raise unprompted is the pricing model. Billed per run, caps protect margin; on a subscription, they protect the business from one heavy user; on passed-through usage, they protect the customer and must be visible, adjustable and alerted before they trip. Same mechanism, three different products — and that decides whether a trip is silent, surfaced or a support conversation.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We cap each run at $2, so spend is controlled."

✅ Reality: That bounds one trajectory. Exposure is the cap times concurrent runs, and concurrency is usually whatever the retry policy allows. Without a tenant budget and a concurrency bound, the per-run cap bounds nothing that appears on the invoice.

❌ Trap: "The provider's cost API tells us what we've spent, so we'll enforce on that."

✅ Reality: Usage lags minutes and cost is daily. That's reconciliation data. Enforcement counts locally from the usage block of each response, at request time.

❌ Trap: "The cap tripped, so the control worked."

✅ Reality: Only if what happened next was designed. A 429 mid-run that the client retries turns a spend cap into a spend amplifier, and a hard failure where a partial answer had value turns a cost control into an outage.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Rate limiting quota & API-level multi-tenancy — the quota mechanisms this note places and scopes.

  • cost modeling — what the cap is denominated in.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Which budgets you set, and what happens when one trips — the same trip branch, one layer in.

  • §10 Cost per call, per task, or per successful task — the gateway that enforces is the gateway that attributes.

  • §7 What the queue does when it can't keep up — the concurrency bound that makes exposure calculable.

  • §2 Where authority to act lives — a gateway in the call path is the same chokepoint argument applied to money.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — the three-layer answer above is the design.

  • §14 Deep research agent — long, expensive runs make the per-run cap the user-visible product boundary.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The dimensions a provider will attribute by — and the ones it won't — Anthropic: Usage and Cost Admin API

  • The non-token lines that belong in the denominator too — Anthropic pricing: feature-specific pricing

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Cost, Latency & Token Budget as Eval Axes — treating cost as a measured axis rather than an afterthought.

  • cost modeling — what a single run costs.

What this note adds: the denominator argument. Every cost figure is a ratio, and the only denominator that can't be gamed is a successful task — plus the attribution constraint that decides whether you can compute it at all.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The denominator that matters? A successful task — failures and retries included in the numerator.
Why provider attribution isn't enough? It groups by credential, not by feature or end user.
What belongs in the numerator besides tokens? Failed runs, retries, tool and search charges, human fallback.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I quote cost per successful task, because every other denominator can be improved by making the system worse. Cost per call drops when you split one call into three. Cost per task drops when you let tasks fail cheaply. Only cost per successful task moves in the right direction for every real improvement, and it's the one the business already thinks in — it compares directly against what the task costs a human. The pivot is attribution: providers group spend by API key, workspace and model, so if you want it per feature or per customer you have to mint credentials along those lines or meter it yourself.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Cost per call Debugging a single prompt. Never as a headline. Rewards splitting work into more, smaller calls. The number improved but the invoice didn't.
Cost per task Early, when success isn't measurable yet. Cheap failures look like savings. Falling cost alongside rising escalations.
Cost per successful task Anything you report or optimise against. The default. Needs a success definition you're willing to defend. —
Fully-loaded cost per outcome Pricing the product, or comparing against a human. Pulls in human review time and support load. Finance asks what a resolution actually costs.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Per call None. Optimises the wrong direction. Dashboards that improve while spend rises.
Per task A run id threaded through every call. Retries become visible; failures don't. Needs a failure rate beside it or it misleads.
Per successful task A verdict recorded per run, and cost joined to it. Failed spend lands in the numerator, where it belongs. Success definition becomes a reviewed artefact, not a guess.
Fully loaded Human-review time attributed to the runs that caused it. The only figure comparable to a human doing the task. A finance conversation, and a number you can price against.

The change that matters is small and structural: a run id on every call, and a recorded verdict per run. Without those two, none of the better denominators are computable, and you're left with whatever the provider's console groups by.

The attribution constraint. Provider reporting groups by API key, workspace, model and service tier — not by feature, tenant or end user. So per-feature cost exists only if you mint a credential per feature, or meter it yourself at the gateway from each response's usage block. The provider's numbers stay authoritative for reconciliation; yours are the ones with the dimensions you actually need.

What else is in the numerator. Tokens aren't the whole bill. Server-side tools carry their own charges — web search is billed per thousand searches, code execution by container-hour beyond a free allowance, hosted agent sessions by session-hour. A cost-per-task figure built only from token usage will quietly understate any agent that searches or executes code, which is most of them.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Cost per task fell 30% and nobody could find the saving in the invoice."

Root cause. The metric counted every started run in the denominator, and a change to a tool's timeout had increased the number of runs that failed early. Those runs were cheap — they died before the expensive steps — so they dragged the average down while contributing nothing. The real cost of a delivered outcome had risen, because the work still had to happen, just on a retry or a human.

Fix. The denominator became successful runs only, with failed and retried spend kept in the numerator, so the metric moved the same direction as the invoice. Applying it late was awkward because historical runs had no recorded verdict, so there was no comparable baseline — three months of trend data had to be discarded and the regression was only provable going forward.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Cost, Latency & Token Budget as Eval Axes — cost as a measured axis.

  • cost modeling — the per-run figure this divides.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §10 Where the spend cap is enforced — the gateway that enforces is the gateway that attributes.

  • §1 Which metrics you commit to before drawing a single box — this is the cost half of that commitment.

  • §8 Optimising for the best run or for every run — consistency is what a success denominator rewards.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — cost per resolved ticket against the human baseline is the business case.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The 50% discount and the window it buys, stated by the vendor — Anthropic: batch processing

  • The same trade on the other major API, for comparison — OpenAI: Batch API guide

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Cost optimization — batching and self-hosting among the cost levers.

What this note adds: the eligibility test and the break-even. Batch is a 50% discount you can only spend if nothing waits on the result, and self-hosting is a fixed cost that beats an API only past a utilisation you should compute before anyone builds it.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What batch costs you? Latency — up to a 24-hour window, no partial results.
Why most agents can't use it? A step's result feeds the next step; the loop can't wait.
Self-host break-even? Fixed hourly cost ÷ per-token saving = tokens/hour you must sustain.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Batch is a straight 50% off both input and output, and the only thing it asks is that nobody is waiting — batches are promised within 24 hours, often much sooner. That rules out the agent loop itself, because step two needs step one's answer, and rules in everything around it: evals, backfills, summarisation, embedding refreshes, offline classification. Self-hosting is a different kind of decision — it converts a variable cost into a fixed one, so it only wins above a sustained utilisation, and I'd want that number computed against real traffic before it's on a diagram at all.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Sync API Anything a user or a next step waits on. The default. Full list price. Interactive traffic, or a loop with data dependencies.
Batch API Nothing waits, and a 24-hour window is acceptable. Latency, and no result until the batch finishes. Nightly jobs, eval runs, backfills, bulk classification.
Self-hosted weights Sustained high volume, or data/latency constraints an API can't meet. Fixed spend regardless of traffic, plus serving expertise. Utilisation high and flat; a residency requirement.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Sync None. Variable, scales to zero. Nothing extra.
Batch A submit/poll/collect path and somewhere to hold results. Halves those workloads. A job that can be late, and a plan for what happens if it is.
Self-host Inference serving you own — autoscaling, batching, model updates. Fixed hourly cost; marginal token cost near zero. On-call for inference; capacity planning; your own upgrade path.

The batch row changes the shape of a workload rather than the architecture of the agent, which is why it's usually the easiest 50% available — and why it's worth separating the parts of a system that must be synchronous from the parts that merely always have been.

The self-host break-even. With a fixed serving cost F per hour and a saving of s per token against the API, self-hosting wins above F / s tokens per hour, sustained. Two things usually decide it before the arithmetic does: the load must be flat, because idle GPUs bill the same as busy ones, and the quality of the open model at your task has to be established first — a break-even computed against a model that can't do the job isn't a break-even. The honest answer in a round is to state the formula, name F and s as things you'd measure, and say what utilisation you'd need to see before committing.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We moved the nightly eval to the Batch API and the release train started slipping."

Root cause. The eval was a release gate, and the team treated "most batches complete in under an hour" as the guarantee rather than the observation — the actual commitment is up to 24 hours. Most nights it finished in twenty minutes; on the nights it didn't, the gate blocked a release with nothing to do but wait, and there was no way to retrieve partial results for the subset already processed.

Fix. The gate moved to a small synchronous smoke suite that runs in minutes, with the full batch eval demoted to a nightly report that informs rather than blocks. The saving was kept and the dependency removed. The general shape: batch is safe for work whose deadline is soft, not merely work whose latency is unobserved — and those are easy to confuse until something is waiting on the result.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Cost optimization — the levers this one places.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §2 Where the sync/async line falls — the same boundary, seen from the cost side.

  • §10 Route by step, cascade on failure, or stay on one model — a self-hosted model is another tier on the ladder.

  • §12 Eval and observability — evals are the workload batch fits best.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Document processing pipeline — almost entirely batch-eligible, which is most of its cost story.
